Unit 07 — The Landscape: Why Some Businesses Are Just Better (Moats)

For a beginner. Arc C (the competitive landscape). New idea: some businesses stay highly profitable for years because they have a moat — a durable advantage rivals can't easily copy. Others have their profits competed away. This is your bridge to strategy.

Plain words first (read once)

  • Margin — profit kept per dollar of sales (Unit 01); a high, steady margin is a clue to a moat.
  • Competitive advantage — a reason a company beats rivals.
  • Moat — a durable competitive advantage: something hard for competitors to copy, that protects profits over time (named after the water-filled ditch protecting a castle).
  • Commodity business — one selling something interchangeable, where rivals compete mainly on price, so margins stay thin.
  • Network effect — the product gets more valuable as more people use it (one kind of moat).

① Material — what we're learning

Why do some companies earn fat profits for decades while others scrape by? The answer is the moat. In a normal market, high profits attract competitors who copy you until the profit is competed away — unless you have something they can't replicate. Spotting a moat (or its absence) is the first move of strategy, and you can often see it right in the margins.

② Understanding — the idea in plain language

Your beach lemonade stand makes a great margin. What happens? Others see it and open stands next to you, cutting prices, until nobody makes much — unless you have a moat: - You hold the only permit to sell on that beach (rivals are locked out), - or a secret recipe everyone prefers (they can't copy the product), - or a brand people trust enough to pay more for, - or you're the spot everyone already meets at (the more people come, the more people come — a network effect).

A moat shows up as a margin that stays high year after year instead of getting competed down. No moat → a commodity → thin, fragile margins.

③ Example — Mastercard vs. the cruise lines (real figures)

Mastercard runs a global payment network. Look at its profit margin over time (net income ÷ revenue, real filings):

Year Revenue Profit Net margin
2009 $5.10 B $1.46 B ~29%
2013 $8.35 B $3.12 B ~37%
…and it stayed in a ~30–45% band for over a decade while revenue kept climbing.

Keeping ~35¢ of profit on every dollar, for 15+ years, is extraordinary — and durable. The moat: a network almost impossible to rebuild (more cardholders attract more merchants, which attract more cardholders), plus trusted rails. Rivals can't simply copy it, so the profits survive.

Now contrast the cruise lines / airlines from Units 01–04: thin margins in good years, and catastrophic losses the moment a shock hits (Royal Caribbean swung from a 17% margin to a −262% one in 2020). They sell a fairly interchangeable service, carry huge fixed costs, and have no moat — so their profits are thin and fragile. Same economy, opposite durability — the difference is the moat.

This is the doorway to the strategy canon: notes/canon/canon-helmer-7-powers (the seven kinds of durable moat) and canon-porter-competitive-strategy (why industry structure sets profitability).

④ Application — your turn

A. Spot the moat (no computer needed). Company X has kept a ~30% net margin for 12 straight years; Company Y's margin bounces between +4% and −20%. Which one likely has a moat, and what's your one-line reason? (X — a durably high, steady margin means rivals haven't competed its profits away; that points to a moat.)

B. Name the type. A marketplace where more buyers attract more sellers, which attracts more buyers, is protected by which kind of moat? (A network effect.)

C. Optional — pull it yourself (only if you have this project set up). Compare margins over years: python3 _ingest/edgar.py facts MA vs python3 _ingest/edgar.py facts CCL. No setup? Skip — A–B taught it.

Check yourself

  1. What is a moat, in one line? (A durable advantage rivals can't easily copy, that protects profits over time.)
  2. Why do high profits without a moat tend to fade? (They attract competitors who copy you and compete the profit away.)
  3. Where in the numbers can you often see a moat? (A high margin that stays high year after year.)
